chunks: Inductor impedance at DC vs infinite frequency. The question: What is an inductors impedance at DC vs infinitely high frequency? Plot this behavior.
An inductor is a coil of wire that resists changes in current.
An ideal one has an impedance of j omega L , which grows in proportion to frequency (the j marks a quarter-cycle timing shift).
At DC the frequency is zero, so the impedance is zero and the inductor is just a piece of wire.
At a very high frequency the impedance becomes huge, so the inductor acts like an open circuit. It is the mirror image of a capacitor.
Imagine a heavy turnstile. If you push it slowly and steadily, it turns easily and lets you through. If you try to jerk it back and forth quickly, its weight fights you hard.
The faster you try to change things, the harder it resists. An inductor does the same with current.
The analogy skips real inductors, where stray capacitance makes the behavior change at very high frequency.
The ideal inductor (grey dashed) rises forever; the real one (accent) follows it up to the SRF at 22. 5 megahertz, peaks, then falls with the capacitor's -20 decibels/dec slope.
The capacitor is the mirror: it falls to its ESR at 15. 9 megahertz and then rises as an inductor.
The real inductor's peak is clipped here by a 1 ohms series resistance; in practice AC resistance and core loss cap it much lower.
Impedance ( j omega L ): the AC opposition of an ideal inductor. DC: a steady signal at zero frequency. Short / open: no opposition at all, or complete opposition.
Self-resonant frequency: where a real inductor's winding capacitance takes over. dB per decade: how steeply a curve rises or falls for each tenfold change in frequency.
Take an ideal 10 microhenries inductor. At 1 kilohertz, Z equals 2 pi f L is about 0. 063 ohms. At 1 megahertz it is about 62. 8 ohms. At 100 megahertz it is about 6. 28 kilohms.
Each tenfold rise in frequency gives a tenfold rise in impedance. That is the whole idea.
"An ideal inductor's impedance is j omega L, so at DC it's zero, a short circuit, and as frequency goes to infinity it goes to infinity, an open circuit.
On a log-log plot that's a straight line rising at 20 decibels per decade. Time-domain, v equals L di/dt: it resists fast current changes.
A real inductor has winding capacitance, so it peaks at its self-resonant frequency and then acts like a capacitor.
The capacitor is the mirror image: open at DC, short at high frequency."
